headline: Connecticut launches TV-to-Table trail linking food-show fame to local restaurants
dek: The new tourism guide highlights more than 60 Connecticut restaurants and chefs featured on national food programs, with a Stamford launch hosted by Waterbury native Scott Conant.
body: Connecticut has turned its television food cameos into a statewide tourism itinerary. Gov. Ned Lamont and the Connecticut Office of Statewide Marketing and Tourism announced the launch of the [Connecticut TV-to-Table Trail](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-announces-tv-to-table-trail) on Oct. 5, inviting visitors to go from watching a chef or restaurant on screen to visiting the place where the food is made.

The program is built as a promotional guide rather than a single road route. The state’s [CTVisit directory](https://ctvisit.com/articles/connecticut-tv-table-trail) presents the trail as a map of restaurants and food destinations that have appeared on television, giving travelers a way to search for stops across Connecticut. The launch announcement says the featured businesses include chefs who have appeared on Chopped, Beat Bobby Flay, Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives, Best Bite in Town, Guy’s Grocery Games and Cupcake Wars.

The breadth is part of the pitch. The [Hour reported](https://www3.thehour.com/food/article/connecticut-tv-table-trail-22454768.php) before the launch that more than 60 eateries were included, spread across Fairfield, Hartford, New Haven, New London, Tolland and other Connecticut counties. The list ranges from Greenwich restaurants such as Colony Grill and Corbo’s Southside Deli to Bridgeport’s Merritt Canteen, Fairfield’s Rawley’s Drive-In and New Haven’s Da Legna X Nolo. Those examples make the trail less about one celebrity destination and more about connecting familiar local businesses with a statewide audience.

The launch took place at the Stamford Museum and Nature Center and featured Connecticut native Scott Conant, a James Beard Award-winning chef, restaurateur, cookbook author and longtime television personality. According to [CT Insider’s preview of the launch](https://www.ctinsider.com/food/article/connecticut-tv-to-table-trail-scott-conant-22427700.php), the event included tastings and a live cooking competition, with one invited guest serving as a judge alongside Conant. The governor’s release says contestants used Conant’s Martone Street tomato sauce with ingredients from farms in Easton and Shelton.

Conant’s role gives the state’s marketing effort a recognizable host, but the trail’s value depends on the restaurants that visitors can actually reach. A TV appearance can create curiosity; a directory can turn that curiosity into a trip to a diner, pizzeria, seafood restaurant or bakery in a different part of the state. For communities outside the major tourism centers, that is a way to attach national exposure to an existing local business without pretending that every stop offers the same kind of dining experience.

The trail also fits a pattern in Connecticut’s tourism strategy. The state has previously promoted themed experiences such as the Connecticut Pizza Trail and the Connecticut Christmas Movie Trail. The TV-to-Table guide uses the same basic idea—organize scattered attractions around a shared theme—but shifts the focus from a single food category or season to restaurants that already have a story connected to television.

For visitors, the immediate next step is to use the CTVisit map to choose stops and then check each business directly for hours, reservations, menus and accessibility. The published material describes the trail as a discovery and marketing tool; it does not promise a uniform pass, discount, ranking or required sequence. That distinction matters because the businesses remain independent restaurants and food destinations, not branches of one state-run attraction.

The launch gives Connecticut a new way to package local food culture, but it does not by itself show how many additional diners the trail will bring. That will depend on whether travelers use the map beyond the initial publicity and whether participating businesses can convert television recognition into repeat visits. For now, the program offers a current, statewide list of places where a familiar television story can become an in-person meal.
location: Stamford Museum and Nature Center, Stamford, Connecticut
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoDescription: Connecticut launched a TV-to-Table tourism trail featuring more than 60 restaurants and chefs seen on national food television programs.
